idiom_name: Adapter : public Target holding an Adaptee member (reference or smart pointer)
implementation_notes: Modern C++ writes the adapter by hand but has a clear default: the object adapter - a class publicly inheriting the target interface (abstract class, or a template constrained by a concept) that holds the adaptee by reference or smart pointer and translates each virtual call. Both the GoF text and current C++ teaching prefer this form because it also adapts adaptee subclasses and works with final classes. The class adapter (public Target + private Adaptee, requiring multiple inheritance) is the alternative when the adaptee's protected members or an overridable member are needed. Where the target is a single callable, std::function is the library-provided type-erasure adapter, and the standard containers std::stack, std::queue and std::priority_queue are themselves container adaptors in the standard's own wording.
pitfalls: A class adapter (private inheritance) pins the concrete adaptee at compile time and silently fails to adapt adaptee subclasses; final/sealed adaptees rule it out entirely.
Holding the adaptee by reference means the adapter can dangle, holding a unique_ptr means it owns it - choose one deliberately and document the lifetime.
Storing the adaptee by value slices subclasses; store a reference, pointer or smart pointer instead.
Virtual dispatch through the target interface adds an indirection: in tight loops call the concrete adaptee directly or make the adapter a template.

variants.name: Class adapter via public interface + private inheritance
variants.implementation_notes: The GoF class adapter: inherit the target interface publicly and the adaptee privately. The adaptee's public members become inaccessible to clients while its protected members and any overridable behaviour stay reachable inside the adapter, and no extra pointer indirection is needed to reach it. Choose this only when you must override or extend the adaptee's behaviour (or reach its protected API); otherwise the object adapter is preferred because it adapts any adaptee subclass and works with final classes.
variants.idiom_name: class Adapter : public Target, private Adaptee
pitfalls: Private inheritance is composition in disguise: do not re-expose the adaptee with `using TextView::getExtent;` unless the target really requires it.
The adapter is welded to one concrete adaptee; a TextView subclass cannot be plugged in without writing another adapter type.
Two inheritance branches invite name-lookup ambiguity - keep exactly one branch that carries implementation and one that carries the interface.

variants.name: Type-erased callable adapter (std::function)
variants.implementation_notes: When the target interface is one callable - a callback, predicate, factory or completion handler - std::function adapts any callable (function pointer, lambda, bind expression, member-function pointer) to a single uniform type, and the adapter object disappears entirely: the closure captures the adaptee. C++11 also brings std::bind and lambdas, which express the same adaptation inline. Prefer this for callback-shaped targets; keep an explicit adapter class when the target has several operations or when the hot path cannot afford std::function's indirect call and possible allocation.
variants.idiom_name: std::function<R(Args...)> wrapping a lambda or function object
pitfalls: std::function may allocate when a capture exceeds its small-buffer and hides the concrete callable's type; measure before putting it on a hot path.
Invoking an empty std::function throws std::bad_function_call, so check a stored callback before calling it.
Capturing by reference into a std::function that outlives the captured object is the C++11 analogue of a dangling callback.
